text_html: A 63-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the office because of a 2-month history of intermittent urinary incontinence and the sensation that “something is falling out of my vagina.” She has had three vaginal deliveries at term. Menopause occurred at the age of 51 years. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 81 kg (178 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows protrusion of the uterus into the vaginal vault. The most likely cause of the pelvic examination findings in this patient is weakness of which of the following muscles and their associated fasciae?
explanation_html:
Educational Objective: Signs and symptoms of uterine prolapse include a vaginal mass, vaginal pressure, perineal discomfort, and urinary or fecal retention or incontinence. Pelvic examination findings in this patient are most likely to identify weakness of the levator ani and coccygeal muscles and their associated fasciae, which help provide pelvic floor support to the uterus.

Evaluation: Uterine prolapse can result from defects in pelvic myofascial support and may be accompanied by other types of pelvic organ prolapse.

Definition: Uterine prolapse results from the loss of connective tissue and muscular support of the uterus, paravaginal tissue, bladder wall, urethra, or distal rectum. The levator ani muscles, the pubococcygeus, puborectalis, and iliococcygeus muscles, in addition to the coccygeus muscle, provide the primary support to the pelvic organs.

Prevention: Risk factors for pelvic support defects include collagen and other connective tissue disorders, vaginal delivery, menopause, prior pelvic surgery, and increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, obesity, chronic constipation).

Treatment: Conservative management may include pelvic floor physical therapy, vaginal pessary, or estrogen therapy. Surgery may be considered in refractory cases.

Differential: This 63-year-old patient with a history of three vaginal deliveries has been identified to have protrusion of the uterus into the vaginal vault on pelvic examination. Weakness of the levator ani and coccygeal muscles and their associated fasciae are the most likely cause of her condition.

Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Choice A: Deep transverse perineal and external urethral sphincter are incorrect. Although the deep transverse perineal muscle and the external urethral sphincter are important to maintain urinary continence, weakness of these structures does not contribute to uterine prolapse. Uterine prolapse is more likely to develop due to weakness of the levator ani and coccygeal muscles.

Choice C: Levator ani and piriformis is incorrect. The piriformis originates from the anterior surface of the sacrum and inserts onto the greater trochanter. Even though the levator ani is involved in uterine support, the piriformis does not contribute to pelvic organ support. Dysfunction of the piriformis may contribute to pelvic or buttock pain.

Choice D: Obturator internus and piriformis is incorrect. The obturator internus originates from the obturator membrane, whereas the piriformis originates from the sacrum. Both muscles insert onto the greater trochanter of the femur and primarily function to externally rotate the thigh. Dysfunction of either muscle does not contribute to the development of uterine prolapse.

options.text_html: Deep transverse perineal and external urethral sphincter
